text: Storyteller's tip, to Silke: a revolt can be called at any step, by anyone, the Warlord included (§16). It needs its caller and two others agreeing on a cause, and the board card lists the causes. Once it's called with two agreeing, play stops until it stands or is dropped. The Emperor may answer it, and it stands only if the caller and two others still back it. One called now, before the tax is paid, voids this year's tax. Under Chaos nobody pays tax, salaries or works, and nobody can buy new land. The harvest, the rent, the auctions and the Warlord carry on. The reserve is sealed: nobody spends it, and it passes whole to whoever is acclaimed. The throne then goes only by acclamation. Anyone but the deposed Emperor may claim it, a peasant or the Warlord included, and the claimants are counted on grain in hand, soldiers on the board and friends.

Thirty from me, Your Majesty, counted out and paid in full. The crown's collector pays first. I'll collect the rest cleanly, and I'll write it all down cleanly too: half the harvest in Year One, and the Warlord refusing outright while he camps on my fields. Five at year's end, I believe you said. I've written that down as well.
W1 stands on G11, the strip below the Wall, beside Province 2 but not on its land.

Thirty, Your Majesty, gladly, and may the Summer Palace have a window facing north-west so you can see your most loyal province. Half is a brave number for Year One, but a brave crown is a strong crown, and I'm always for strength. Clark, count it twice. I'd hate for anyone to say the Gentry came up short.

The Director's direction for your character (not table talk), replacing the earlier note: Greedy and fawning, and he loves the Gentry's seat: the rent, the Harvest Pile, his granary. He flatters the crown while it's strong and counts his friends the moment it wobbles. Pieces are leverage to him, to rent or to sell dear, and he'd rather be the man every claimant needs than the man in the chair. He and the Official have never trusted each other: a man who writes everything down is a man who means to use it.

The Director's direction for your character (not table talk), replacing the earlier note: Ambitious, and he keeps a paper trail. He knows every cause for revolt by heart and notes each one as it comes true. He wants the throne, and he sees the table itself as the ladder to it: a crown the table gives is held by friends. He has never trusted a landlord, and he'd sooner see the chair empty than see the Gentry, or the Gentry's man, in it.

Let's count it out loud. Thirty from me, thirty from Paddy, and the man sitting in the sea off our two coasts pays nothing and puts the kettle on. Half the harvest in Year One buys a Summer Palace I'll never see from the silk fields, while the crown "doesn't knock on tents." If someone calls it on that cause, Your Majesty, I'm backing it. Cut the number to something a coast can live on, or show me the crown can make Rob pay, and I'll pay what I owe gladly.
Thirty each, and that boat is sitting right on our shared shore. If you'll back the Warlord cause with me, Reina has to answer us both, so we squeeze the tax down together. Don't pay until she does.
Silke doesn't pay yet: she says she'd back a revolt on 'the Emperor can't control the Warlord' if someone calls it.

I've got the thirty, Your Majesty, counted out right here, and I'm not one to owe anybody. But there's a boat sitting off my rice fields and the crown won't knock on its tent. So if someone calls it on the Warlord, I'm with Silke. Bring the number down to something a coast can stand, or tell me who keeps that boat off my shore, and I'll pay you before you finish asking.
Paddy doesn't pay yet either: he'd back a revolt on 'the Emperor can't control the Warlord' alongside Silke, if someone calls it.

Well, I can't let the coast do all the brave talking. I call a revolt, and the cause is me: the Emperor can't control the Warlord. Reina, I'm sitting right here, I haven't paid a grain, and the crown "doesn't knock on tents." Silke, Paddy, keep your thirty. And if you'd like the boat moved, we can talk about that once there's nobody on the throne telling us what to do.
Rob calls a revolt on 'the Emperor can't control the Warlord', and Silke and Paddy agree: two others, so the revolt is called. Play stops until it stands or is dropped. No tax has been collected.

Rob, you want the throne to bend over a kettle, and it won't. The rate stands, because a crown that cuts on its first complaint is finished by its second. But Silke and Paddy, your grievance is the boat, not the number, and the crown hears you. The Winter Palace goes up this year instead of the Summer, so the Grand Canal reaches your coasts first. Ten grain each to you, from my own reserve, today, for a coast guard. And while I sit here, the crown pays half of every soldier you raise against him. Ask yourselves who keeps that boat away once there's nobody on the throne. Rob has already told you he'll "talk about it then.

Reina answers: the tax stays at 50%; the work becomes the Winter Palace, with a coast canal section promised next; she pays Silke and Paddy 10 each now from the reserve, and promises half of any soldier a coastal province buys against the Warlord while she reigns.
